title: Chapter 16 — Of Conquest
paragraphs: Although governments can originally have no other origin than the one described earlier, and political societies can be founded on nothing but the consent of the people, ambition has filled the world with such disorders that, in the noise of war, which makes up so great a part of the history of mankind, this consent is little noticed. So many people have mistaken the force of arms for the consent of the people, and count conquest as one of the origins of government. But conquest is as far from setting up any government as demolishing a house is from building a new one in its place. It often makes way, indeed, for a new frame of commonwealth by destroying the old one; but without the consent of the people it can never erect a new one.

All men will readily agree that the aggressor, who puts himself into the state of war with another and unjustly invades another man’s right, can never, by such an unjust war, come to have a right over the conquered. That is, all men will agree who do not think that robbers and pirates have a right of empire over whoever they have force enough to master, or that men are bound by promises which unlawful force extorts from them. Suppose a robber breaks into my house and, with a dagger at my throat, makes me seal deeds conveying my estate to him. Would this give him any title? An unjust conqueror who forces me into submission has just such a title, by his sword. The injury and the crime are the same, whether committed by the wearer of a crown or by some petty villain. The rank of the offender and the number of his followers make no difference to the offence, unless it is to aggravate it. The only difference is that great robbers punish little ones to keep them in obedience, while the great ones are rewarded with laurels and triumphs, because they are too big for the weak hands of justice in this world and have in their own possession the power that ought to punish offenders. What is my remedy against a robber who has broken into my house like that? To appeal to the law for justice. But perhaps justice is denied, or I am crippled and cannot move, or robbed and do not have the means to do it. If God has taken away every means of seeking a remedy, there is nothing left but patience. But my son, when he is able, may seek the relief of the law that is denied to me; he or his son may renew the appeal until he recovers his right. The conquered, however, or their children, have no court and no arbitrator on earth to appeal to. Then they may appeal, as Jephthah did, to heaven, and repeat their appeal until they have recovered the native right of their ancestors, which was to have such a legislative over them as the majority should approve and freely accept. If it is objected that this would cause endless trouble, I answer: no more than justice does, where she is open to all who appeal to her. Whoever troubles his neighbour without cause is punished for it by the justice of the court he appeals to. And whoever appeals to heaven must be sure he has right on his side, and a right, too, that is worth the trouble and cost of the appeal, since he will answer for it at a tribunal that cannot be deceived and will be sure to repay everyone according to the harms he has done to his fellow subjects, that is, to any part of mankind. From all this it is plain that whoever conquers in an unjust war can have no title by it to the subjection and obedience of the conquered.
But supposing victory favours the right side, let us consider a conqueror in a lawful war, and see what power he gets, and over whom.

First, it is plain that by his conquest he gets no power over those who conquered with him. Those who fought on his side cannot lose by the conquest, but must be at least as free as they were before. Most commonly they serve on terms, on condition that they share with their leader and enjoy a part of the spoils and the other advantages that come with the conquering sword; or at least that they have a part of the subdued country given to them. And the conquering people are not, I hope, to be made slaves by conquest, and to wear their laurels only to show that they are sacrifices to their leader’s triumph. Those who found absolute monarchy on the title of the sword turn their heroes, the founders of such monarchies, into out-and-out Drawcansirs, and forget that they had any officers and soldiers who fought on their side in the battles they won, or helped them to subdue, or shared in possessing, the countries they mastered. Some tell us that the English monarchy is founded on the Norman conquest, and that our princes therefore have a title to absolute dominion. Even if that were true (and the history shows otherwise), and William had a right to make war on this island, his dominion by conquest could still reach no further than the Saxons and Britons who were then the inhabitants of this country. The Normans who came with him and helped to conquer, and all who are descended from them, are free men and not subjects by conquest, whatever dominion that conquest may give. And if I, or anybody else, claim freedom as descended from them, it will be very hard to prove the contrary. It is plain, too, that the law, which has made no distinction between the one and the other, does not intend there to be any difference in their freedom or privileges.

But suppose, which seldom happens, that the conquerors and the conquered never merge into one people under the same laws and freedom. Let us see next what power a lawful conqueror has over the subdued; and that, I say, is purely despotic. He has an absolute power over the lives of those who have forfeited them by an unjust war, but not over the lives or fortunes of those who did not take part in the war, nor over the possessions even of those who were actually engaged in it.

Secondly, I say, then, that the conqueror gets power only over those who have actually assisted, concurred in, or consented to the unjust force that is used against him. The people have given their governors no power to do an unjust thing, such as making an unjust war, for they never had such a power in themselves. So they ought not to be charged as guilty of the violence and injustice committed in an unjust war, any further than they actually abet it, any more than they are to be thought guilty of any violence or oppression their governors might use on the people themselves, or on any part of their fellow subjects; for they have empowered them no more to do the one than the other. Conquerors, it is true, seldom trouble themselves to make this distinction; they willingly let the confusion of war sweep everyone together. But that does not alter the right. The conqueror’s power over the lives of the conquered exists only because they have used force to commit or maintain an injustice, so he can have that power only over those who have concurred in that force. All the rest are innocent. He has no more title over the people of that country who have done him no injury, and so have made no forfeiture of their lives, than he has over anyone else who, without any injuries or provocations, has lived on fair terms with him.

Thirdly, the power a conqueror gets over those he overcomes in a just war is perfectly despotic. He has an absolute power over the lives of those who have forfeited them by putting themselves in a state of war; but he does not thereby have a right and title to their possessions. I do not doubt that at first sight this will seem a strange doctrine, since it is so completely contrary to the practice of the world. Nothing is more familiar, when speaking of the dominion of countries, than to say that so-and-so conquered it, as if conquest, without any further ado, conveyed a right of possession. But we should consider that the practice of the strong and powerful, however universal it may be, is seldom the rule of right, even though it is one part of the subjection of the conquered not to argue against the conditions the conquering sword has cut out for them.

In all war there is usually a mixture of force and damage, and the aggressor seldom fails to harm the estate of those he makes war on when he uses force against their persons. Yet it is the use of force alone that puts a man into the state of war. Whether he begins the injury by force, or, having done the injury quietly and by fraud, refuses to make reparation and maintains it by force (which is the same as having done it by force in the first place), it is the unjust use of force that makes the war. Someone who breaks open my house and violently turns me out of doors, and someone who gets in peaceably and then keeps me out by force, in effect do the same thing. That is supposing we are in such a state that we have no common judge on earth whom I may appeal to and whom we are both obliged to submit to, for that is the case I am now speaking of. It is the unjust use of force, then, that puts a man into the state of war with another, and by it whoever is guilty of it forfeits his life. For in abandoning reason, which is the rule given between man and man, and using force, the way of beasts, he becomes liable to be destroyed by the one he uses force against, like any savage, ravenous beast that is dangerous to his existence.

But the father’s misdeeds are not the children’s faults, and they may be rational and peaceable in spite of the brutishness and injustice of the father. So the father, by his misdeeds and violence, can forfeit only his own life, and does not involve his children in his guilt or destruction. His goods, which nature, willing the preservation of all mankind as far as possible, has made to belong to the children to keep them from perishing, still continue to belong to his children. For supposing they did not join in the war, whether through infancy, absence, or choice, they have done nothing to forfeit them. Nor does the conqueror have any right to take them away merely on the ground of having subdued the man who attempted his destruction by force; though perhaps he may have some right to them to repair the damages he has suffered from the war and from the defence of his own right. How far that reaches to the possessions of the conquered we shall see shortly. So whoever has, by conquest, a right over a man’s person to destroy him if he pleases, does not thereby have a right over his estate to possess and enjoy it. For it is the brutal force the aggressor has used that gives his adversary a right to take away his life and destroy him, if he pleases, as a noxious creature; but it is damage suffered that alone gives him a title to another man’s goods. I may kill a thief who attacks me on the highway; yet I may not (which seems a lesser thing) take away his money and let him go. That would be robbery on my part. His force, and the state of war he put himself in, made him forfeit his life, but gave me no title to his goods. The right of conquest, then, extends only to the lives of those who joined in the war, and not to their estates, except in order to make reparation for the damages received and the costs of the war; and even that is subject to reserving the right of the innocent wife and children.

Let the conqueror have as much justice on his side as can be imagined; he still has no right to seize more than the vanquished could forfeit. The vanquished man’s life is at the victor’s mercy, and the victor may take his service and goods to make himself reparation. But he cannot take the goods of his wife and children. They too had a title to the goods he enjoyed, and their shares in the estate he possessed. For example, suppose that I, in the state of nature (and all commonwealths are in the state of nature with one another), have injured another man and, refusing to give satisfaction, have brought things to a state of war, in which my defending by force what I had gained unjustly makes me the aggressor. I am conquered. My life, it is true, is forfeit and at his mercy, but not the lives of my wife and children. They did not make the war, nor did they assist in it. I could not forfeit their lives; they were not mine to forfeit. My wife had a share in my estate, and I could not forfeit that either. And my children also, being born of me, had a right to be maintained out of my labour or substance. Here, then, is the case: the conqueror has a title to reparation for damages received, and the children have a title to their father’s estate for their subsistence. (As for the wife’s share, whether her own labour or a compact gave her a title to it, it is plain that her husband could not forfeit what was hers.) What must be done in this case? I answer: since the fundamental law of nature is that all, as far as possible, should be preserved, it follows that if there is not enough to satisfy both fully, namely the conqueror’s losses and the children’s maintenance, the one who has enough and to spare must give up something of his full satisfaction, and give way to the pressing and stronger title of those who are in danger of perishing without it.

But suppose the costs and damages of the war are to be made up to the conqueror to the last penny, and that the children of the vanquished, stripped of all their father’s goods, are to be left to starve and perish. Even so, satisfying what is due to the conqueror on this account will hardly give him a title to any country he conquers. For the damages of war can hardly amount to the value of any considerable tract of land in any part of the world where all the land is possessed and none lies waste. And if I have not taken away the conqueror’s land (which, since I am the one vanquished, I cannot possibly have done), hardly any other damage I have done him can amount to the value of my land, supposing mine is equally cultivated and of an extent at all close to what I had overrun of his. The destruction of a year’s produce, or two (for it seldom reaches four or five), is the most damage that can usually be done. As for money, and such riches and treasure taken away, these are not nature’s goods; they have only a fanciful, imaginary value. Nature has put no such value on them. By her standard they are worth no more than the wampompeke of the Americans to a European prince, or than the silver money of Europe would once have been to an American. And five years’ produce is not worth the perpetual inheritance of land where all is possessed and none remains waste, to be taken up by the one who has been dispossessed. This will easily be granted if one only sets aside the imaginary value of money, for the disproportion is greater than that between five and five hundred. At the same time, though, half a year’s produce is worth more than the inheritance where there is more land than the inhabitants possess and use, and anyone is at liberty to make use of the waste; but there conquerors take little trouble to possess themselves of the lands of the vanquished. So no damage that men in the state of nature (as all princes and governments are in relation to one another) suffer from one another can give a conqueror power to dispossess the descendants of the vanquished and turn them out of that inheritance, which ought to be the possession of them and their descendants to all generations. The conqueror will indeed be inclined to think himself master, and it is the very condition of the subdued not to be able to dispute their right. But if that is all, it gives no title other than what bare force gives the stronger over the weaker; and by that reasoning, whoever is strongest will have a right to whatever he pleases to seize.

Over those, then, who joined with him in the war, and over those of the subdued country who did not oppose him, and even over the descendants of those who did, the conqueror has no right of dominion by his conquest, even in a just war. They are free from any subjection to him, and if their former government is dissolved, they are at liberty to begin and set up another for themselves.

The conqueror, it is true, usually uses the force he has over them to compel them, with a sword at their breasts, to bow to his conditions and submit to whatever government he pleases to give them. But the question is, what right does he have to do so? If it is said that they submit by their own consent, then this admits that their own consent is necessary to give the conqueror a title to rule over them. It remains only to consider whether promises extorted by force, without right, can be counted as consent, and how far they bind. To this I say that they do not bind at all, because whatever another gets from me by force, I still keep the right to, and he is obliged to restore it at once. If someone takes my horse from me by force, he ought to return it at once, and I still have a right to take it back. By the same reasoning, if someone forced a promise from me, he ought to give it back at once, that is, release me from its obligation; or I may take it back myself, that is, choose whether I will keep it. For the law of nature lays obligations on me only through the rules she prescribes, so she cannot oblige me through the violation of her rules; and extorting anything from me by force is exactly such a violation. Nor does it change the case at all to say, “I gave my promise,” any more than it excuses the force and passes the right when I put my hand in my pocket and hand my purse over myself to a thief who demands it with a pistol at my chest.

From all this it follows that the government of a conqueror, imposed by force on the subdued, whether on those against whom he had no right of war, or on those who did not join in the war against him where he did have right, lays no obligation on them.

But let us suppose that all the men of that community, being all members of the same body politic, may be taken to have joined in the unjust war in which they are subdued, and so their lives are at the conqueror’s mercy.

I say this does not concern their children who are still minors. Since a father does not himself have a power over the life or liberty of his child, no act of his can possibly forfeit it. So the children, whatever may have happened to the fathers, are free men, and the absolute power of the conqueror reaches no further than the persons of the men he subdued, and dies with them. And even if he governs those men as slaves, subjected to his absolute arbitrary power, he has no such right of dominion over their children. He can have no power over the children except by their own consent, whatever he may drive them to say or do; and he has no lawful authority as long as force, and not choice, compels them to submit.

Every man is born with a double right. First, a right of freedom for his person, over which no other man has any power; the free disposal of it lies in himself. Secondly, a right, before any other man, to inherit his father’s goods together with his brothers and sisters.

By the first of these, a man is naturally free from subjection to any government, even if he is born in a place under its jurisdiction. But if he disowns the lawful government of the country he was born in, he must also give up the right that belonged to him by its laws, and the possessions there that came down to him from his ancestors, if it was a government made by their consent.

By the second, the inhabitants of any country who are descended from those who were subdued and had a government forced on them against their free consent, and who derive a title to their estates from them, keep a right to the possessions of their ancestors, even though they do not freely consent to the government whose harsh conditions were imposed by force on the owners of that country. For the first conqueror never had a title to the land of that country. So the people who are descended from, or claim under, those who were forced by constraint to submit to the yoke of a government always have a right to shake it off and free themselves from the usurpation or tyranny which the sword has brought upon them, until their rulers place them under a frame of government to which they willingly and by choice consent. Who doubts that the Grecian Christians, descendants of the ancient owners of that country, may justly throw off the Turkish yoke, under which they have groaned so long, whenever they have the opportunity? For no government can have a right to obedience from a people who have not freely consented to it. And they can never be supposed to have done so until either they are put in a full state of liberty to choose their government and governors, or at least until they have standing laws to which they have given their free consent, by themselves or their representatives, and also until they are allowed their due property. That means being owners of what they have in such a way that nobody can take away any part of it without their own consent. Without this, men under any government are not in the state of free men, but are outright slaves under the force of war.

But grant that the conqueror in a just war has a right to the estates of the conquered, as well as power over their persons; which, it is plain, he does not. Even so, no absolute power will follow from it in the continuance of the government. For the descendants of these people are all free men, and if he grants them estates and possessions to live on in his country (without which it would be worth nothing), then whatever he grants them, they have property in, as far as it is granted. And the nature of property is that it cannot be taken from a man without his own consent.

Their persons are free by a native right, and their properties, whether more or less, are their own and at their own disposal, not at his; otherwise it is not property. Suppose the conqueror gives one man a thousand acres, to him and his heirs for ever, and leases another man a thousand acres for his life, at a rent of £50 or £500 a year. Does the first not have a right to his thousand acres for ever, and the second a right to his during his life, as long as he pays that rent? And does the tenant for life not have a property in everything he gains over and above his rent by his labour and industry during that term, supposing it is double the rent? Can anyone say that the king, or conqueror, after his grant, may by his power as conqueror take away all or part of the land from the heirs of the one, or from the other during his life while he pays the rent? Or can he take away from either of them, at his pleasure, the goods or money they have earned on that land? If he can, then all free and voluntary contracts cease and are void in the world. Nothing is needed to dissolve them at any time but enough power, and all the grants and promises of men in power are only mockery and collusion. For can there be anything more ridiculous than to say, “I give you and yours this for ever, and in the surest and most solemn form of conveyance that can be devised,” and yet for it to be understood that I have a right, if I please, to take it away from you again tomorrow?

I will not argue now about whether princes are exempt from the laws of their country. But this I am sure of: they owe subjection to the laws of God and nature. Nobody and no power can exempt them from the obligations of that eternal law. Those obligations are so great and so strong in the case of promises that omnipotence itself can be bound by them. Grants, promises, and oaths are bonds that hold the Almighty, whatever some flatterers tell the princes of the world, who all together, with all their people joined to them, are, in comparison with the great God, only as a drop of the bucket or a dust on the balance: insignificant, nothing!

In short, the case of conquest is this. The conqueror, if he has a just cause, has a despotic right over the persons of all who actually aided and concurred in the war against him, and a right to make up his damages and costs out of their labour and estates, provided he does not injure the right of anyone else. Over the rest of the people, if there were any who did not consent to the war, and over the children of the captives themselves, or the possessions of either, he has no power. So he can have, by virtue of conquest, no lawful title to dominion over them himself, nor pass one on to his descendants. Instead he is an aggressor if he makes attempts on their properties, and thereby puts himself in a state of war against them. And neither he nor any of his successors has any better right of rule than Hingar or Hubba, the Danes, had here in England, or than Spartacus would have had if he had conquered Italy; which is to say, a right to have their yoke thrown off as soon as God gives those under their subjection the courage and opportunity to do it. So, whatever title the kings of Assyria had over Judah by the sword, God helped Hezekiah to throw off the dominion of that conquering empire. “And the Lord was with Hezekiah, and he prospered; wherefore he went forth, and he rebelled against the king of Assyria, and served him not” (2 Kings xviii. 7). From this it is plain that shaking off a power which force, and not right, has set over anyone, though it bears the name of rebellion, is no offence before God. It is something he allows and approves, even where promises and covenants obtained by force have intervened. For it is very probable, to anyone who reads the story of Ahaz and Hezekiah attentively, that the Assyrians subdued Ahaz and deposed him, and made Hezekiah king in his father’s lifetime; and that Hezekiah, by agreement, had done him homage and paid him tribute all this time.
